name: E. coli Acid Resistance
description: E. coli has evolved sophisticated mechanisms to survive highly acidic environments encountered in its host (e.g., stomach) or during food processing. This computational flowchart details the primary acid resistance (AR) systems. Under mild acid stress (pH 4.5-5.5) and in log phase, the **AR1 system** is activated, primarily driven by the general stress sigma factor RpoS, which upregulates a suite of general stress proteins. For more severe acid stress (pH < 2.5), particularly in stationary phase, the robust **AR2 system** becomes critical. This system relies on amino acid decarboxylases (e.g., GadA/B for glutamate, CadA for lysine, AdiA for arginine) which consume intracellular protons, converting amino acids into their neutral decarboxylated products (GABA, cadaverine, agmatine). Cognate antiporters (GadC, CadB, AdiC) then export these products while simultaneously importing fresh amino acids, effectively buffering the cytoplasm. The activation of the lysine-dependent system, for instance, involves a specific proteolytic cleavage of its transcriptional regulator, CadC, in response to acid. The **AR3 system**, an arginine-dependent pathway, operates similarly but is active during log phase. Concurrently, modifications to key cell envelope structures, including LPS, outer membrane proteins, and peptidoglycan, provide an additional layer of protection by reducing proton permeability. These interconnected strategies collectively ensure E. coli's survival and internal pH homeostasis in challenging acidic conditions.
